### 2026-10-24: In this session, I made some test programs for the different components on my Mini Piano to verify if they work well when I get them and started on the main program to run for all of the components. I

**1h**

In this session, I made some test programs for the different components on my Mini Piano to verify if they work well when I get them and started on the main program to run for all of the components. I had to use some AI to learn some of how the micro python works, but I tried to have it teach me as much as possible rather than copy pasting. I used Hackatime to track the hours, but I had more time on here because of the code I did on my school computer, where hackatime is blocked.

Making the test programs, mainly on my school computer, took a long time because I had to learn how the micro python code for it worked and then code it all for all 5 of the types of components I was using.

### 2026-10-25: In this session, I replaced some mismatched components in Easyeda and Digikey and I added to the code by creating variables and some of the inputs.

**0.58h**

In this session, I replaced some mismatched components in Easyeda and Digikey and I added to the code by creating variables and some of the inputs.

First, I replaced the mismatched components in Easyeda. This I logged with the timelapse included, so I shouldn't have to say much more than that I replaced the Pico SC0915 on Digikey with the newer SC1631, the rotary encoder with an EC11 style one on Digikey, and the switches in Easyeda for the ones I had on Digikey.

Second, I made some variables in my code. I used a dictionary for the hertz values (named notesHz) corresponding to the note name (excluding flats and instead just using their sharp equivalents) so I could use it both to make it easier to play the hertz on the speaker based off of the name of the note and so I could index notesHz.keys() with which key is being pressed, tying the pad number to the note.
Then, I made the input code for the capacitive touch sensors and the switches. I had to use both a list of the keys currently being pressed and a variable for the key most recently pressed so I could play only the most recently pressed key (the piezo doesn't allow me to play chords). Then I just had it do this: For each key, if it is just now being pressed set lastKeyPressed to the key and append it to keysPressed, else delete it from keysPressed (now I realize I made a logic error here I'll have to fix later). Then for the switches I just had a variable for each one and set that to True if the value for the key equaled 0.

### 2026-10-25: In this session, I made the code for the while loop in the main program.

**0.1h**

In this session, I made the code for the while loop in the main program.

I improved the logic for all of the code, from the switches with debouncing and having them now just updating the octaves and mode instead of using extra variables, to the led outputs, to the speaker output, to clamping variable values with volume, octaves, and modes, to making the actual mode logic.

I used AI for some debugging throughout since I was unable to run it since I didn't have any board to run it on, but I did all of the actual code myself, I just used it to find out what was wrong.

I chose to use 3 modes for the Mini Piano, the first being just a normal mode where it plays the note until you release the key, the second being a sort of synth mode where it plays the single note even after you release it for about 2 seconds, and the third being an experimental mode I wanted to try where it plays the note of the average hertz values of all of the keys currently being pressed. It will probably sound terrible, but I just wanted to see how that would work.

Sorry for the lack of the detail, I know I did a lot in this session, but I don't have much time before the deadline for Week 3 to explain what I did and I already forgot some of it even though I did it all in one day. I also may have changed the code a little if I found more errors with it after this, like in modes 1 and 2.
